title: Matryoshka embeddings
summary: Naive truncation of an ordinary embedding collapses to 0.209 recall at 32 dimensions, because the information is spread evenly across all of them. A free rotation more than doubles that, and Matryoshka training buys the same property as a property of the model rather than a per-corpus artefact you have to version.
html:
Six days of compression, all of it the same shape: the model emits a vector, then you throw some of it away. Today is a different idea. Change the training so that the first half of the vector is already a vector, and compression becomes a slice.

Why you cannot just truncate

Take the first k dimensions of a normal embedding and see what survives. Measured on the usual corpus:

dims   bytes   recall@10 from a naive prefix
  32     128                          0.209
  64     256                          0.391
 128     512                          0.574
 256    1024                          0.776
 384    1536                          1.000

Half the vector gives you 0.574. A twelfth of it gives 0.209, which is close to useless.

The reason is something you already measured. On Day 24, checking whether PQ subspaces were imbalanced, the variance across contiguous blocks came out at a ratio of 1.16, essentially flat. The information is spread evenly across all 384 dimensions. There is nothing special about the first 32, so taking them gives you a twelfth of the signal, which is exactly what the table shows.

The post-hoc fix, which you already have

If the problem is that importance is spread evenly, concentrate it. Day 24 established that an orthogonal rotation is free: it preserves every distance, so you can apply one and lose nothing. Rotate so the leading directions carry the most variance, then truncate:

dims    naive prefix    rotated prefix
  32           0.209             0.452
  64           0.391             0.632
 128           0.574             0.800
 256           0.776             0.954
 384           1.000             1.000

At 32 dimensions the rotation more than doubles recall. At 256 it takes you from 0.776 to 0.954, which is a quarter of the storage for four points.

Two details worth having. Use the uncentered decomposition, an SVD of the matrix rather than an eigendecomposition of the covariance. Textbook PCA subtracts the mean first, and subtracting a mean is not a rotation, so it changes your cosine geometry: my centered version scored 0.914 at full rank instead of 1.000. The uncentered version is a pure rotation and reproduces the exact ranking at full width, as it must.

And this costs nothing at query time. One matrix multiply against a cache-resident matrix, which Day 24 already priced at 576 KB.

What Matryoshka adds

So if a free rotation gets you most of the way, what is MRL for?

The training objective. A normal model optimises a contrastive loss on the full vector. Matryoshka Representation Learning optimises it at several prefix lengths at once:

L = L_contrastive(x[:64])
  + L_contrastive(x[:128])
  + L_contrastive(x[:256])
  + L_contrastive(x[:512])
  + L_contrastive(x[:768])

Every prefix is scored as an embedding in its own right, so gradients push the model to put coarse, broadly useful distinctions in the early dimensions and refinements later. The nesting is in the name: each prefix is a complete smaller embedding with a bigger one wrapped around it.

The difference from rotating is not mainly about how much recall you keep at a given width. It is about what the property belongs to:

  • A rotation is fitted to your corpus. Change the corpus and the right rotation changes, and you have another artefact to version, recompute and keep in sync with the index. Get it out of sync and queries land in a different basis than documents, silently.
  • MRL is a property of the model. Truncation works on any corpus, with no fitted object, no extra state and nothing to desynchronise. Slice and go.

For a system you have to operate rather than demo, that is the real argument. One fewer fitted artefact in the pipeline is worth more than a couple of points of recall.

What it costs the model

Nothing is free, so ask what the extra loss terms take away. The full-width embedding is now optimised alongside four shorter ones rather than on its own, which means the widest vector from an MRL model is in principle slightly worse than the same architecture trained only at full width.

Reported degradation is small, usually described as a fraction of a point, and the published argument is that the prefix objectives act a little like regularisation rather than pure competition. I have not measured this and I am repeating it, so treat it as the claim it is. If you are choosing between two models and one is MRL-trained, compare them at full width on your own data rather than assuming the capability is costless.

The honest framing is a trade you are almost always happy to make: give up a sliver of peak quality to gain the ability to run the same model at a quarter of the width whenever you want to.

Adaptive retrieval

The pattern is the one from Days 21 and 27, with the cheapest possible first stage:

1. search with 64-dim prefixes      256 B/vector, in memory
2. take the top few hundred
3. rescore with the full vectors     1536 B/vector, from wherever they live
4. return top k

What makes it nicer than PQ is that there is no decode and no codebook. The short vector is a prefix of the long one, so the two tiers are the same array read to different lengths. You can keep one copy of the full vectors and slice at whatever width the current query deserves, changing the operating point per request without re-indexing anything.

Try that with PQ and you need a second set of codes at a second value of m.

Limits and honesty

My numbers measure a model that was not MRL-trained, so the naive and rotated rows are real but the MRL row is missing. I tried to load two MRL models to complete the table and hit a dependency conflict with one and a download that outran my time budget on the other. So take the mechanism and the published claim (MRL models hold most of their quality down to a quarter or an eighth of their width) as reported rather than reproduced here.

What I did verify is the part that motivates it: truncation of an ordinary embedding fails badly, the failure is explained by the flat variance I measured on Day 24, and a free rotation fixes most of it. The case for MRL is that it gives you the same benefit without a per-corpus artefact.

Phase 2 has now made vectors findable and small. There is one assumption running through all of it that production breaks immediately: that a query wants the nearest neighbours out of everything. Real queries come with a tenant id and a date range. Tomorrow: filtered search, the trap everyone hits.
exercise:
1. Measure your own truncation curve. Take your embeddings, slice the first 32, 64, 128 and 256 dimensions, renormalise each, and measure recall@10 against the full-width ranking. If your model is not MRL-trained this will look bad, and the shape of bad is worth seeing.

2. Add the free rotation. Compute an uncentered SVD of your matrix, project both documents and queries, and rerun the same curve. Confirm full width still reproduces 1.000, which is your check that you did a rotation and not a projection. Then compare the two curves at 64 dimensions.

3. Check whether your model supports it properly. Look up whether the embedding model you plan to use was trained with Matryoshka losses, and if so what widths it supports. If it was, you get the Day 27 int8 saving and this one multiplicatively: a 768-dim float32 vector at 3072 bytes becomes a 192-dim int8 vector at 192 bytes, which is 16x before any quantizer is involved.
